analysis.one_liner: Blocks EPA from tightening ground-level ozone pollution limits until most dirty counties meet the current limit.
analysis.headline: Backed by 70 House members (68 Republicans, 2 Democrats), the bill never got a hearing or vote; it was referred to a House Energy and Commerce subcommittee three days after introduction and died there when the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have stopped the EPA from lowering its national limit on ground-level ozone — the main ingredient in smog — until at least 85% of counties over the current limit had come into compliance. It also would have forced the EPA to designate dirty counties only where an actual air monitor shows a violation (not computer modeling), to weigh industry compliance costs against health protection, and to calculate the rule's benefits without counting reductions in other pollutants. It never left committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Industries that emit the chemicals that form ozone — refiners, oil and gas producers, coal-fired power plants, and manufacturers in polluted regions. The bill delays or prevents a tighter ozone limit, which would mean fewer counties labeled as violating air standards, fewer expensive pollution permits, and less required emissions control.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Refiners, oil and gas, utilities, manufacturers

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits the EPA from setting a lower ozone standard until at least 85% of counties violating the current standard achieve full compliance, tying public-health protection to the pace of polluting counties' cleanup [S2][S3]
Requires the EPA to find a county out of compliance only on the basis of direct air-quality monitoring rather than modeling, which would shrink the number of regulated areas [S2][S3]
Requires the EPA to take feasibility and cost into account when setting the ozone standard, a change from the Clean Air Act's health-first framework [S2][S3]

Requires a regulatory impact analysis that excludes benefits from reducing pollutants other than ozone — though the emissions that create ozone also create other harmful pollution — so the required analysis would understate the health benefits of a tighter rule [S3]

analysis.who_pays: People who breathe ozone pollution: the bill delays a tighter smog limit, and ozone is linked to asthma attacks, worsened lung disease, and premature deaths. People in counties the EPA might have designated as violating air standards based on monitoring data plus modeling would also lose that protection.

drawbacks.text: Under the bill, an area proven by modeling to exceed the ozone limit but lacking a monitor showing a violation could not be designated a nonattainment area, leaving it unregulated [S2][S3]

Delaying a tighter ozone standard until 85% of dirty counties comply with the old standard means people in remaining polluted counties keep breathing smog above the level health scientists identified [S2]

The bill's own requirement that the EPA weigh feasibility and cost acknowledges the burden supporters were protecting: tighter standards force new pollution permits and emissions controls on industry, which supporters argued would raise costs for local economies [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered real savings to industry and local governments that would otherwise face new pollution permits and controls under a tighter ozone limit. The cost falls on public health: a tighter smog limit prevents asthma attacks and premature deaths, and the bill's requirement to count only direct monitors, ignore cleanup pace, and exclude co-benefits from the required analysis would each make the standard weaker. On the record before us, the bill's protections accrue to polluting industries and its costs to people who breathe the air.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Energy and Power subcommittee three days later, and nothing ever happened to it again; it died when the 114th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Pete Olson introduced the bill on March 17, 2015, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day [S1][S5]
Three days later, on March 20, 2015, it was referred to the subcommittee on Energy and Power, where it stayed [S5]

Sixty-nine members cosponsored the bill — 67 Republicans and 2 Democrats — but the subcommittee never acted, no hearing or vote occurred, and the bill never reached the House floor before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017 [S4][S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People who breathe ozone pollution came out ahead: because the bill never advanced, the EPA remained free to tighten the standard, which it did in 2015. The refiners, utilities, and manufacturers the bill would have shielded from a stricter limit did not get that protection.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Ozone-polluted areas got the tighter EPA standard

for.name: Rep. Pete Olson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited cosponsors

sides.party_line_note: Support was almost entirely Republican — 67 of the bill's 69 cosponsors were House Republicans — but the bill never reached a vote, so no opposition was ever recorded on the floor.

industries.industry: Oil and gas producers and refiners
industries.note: A tighter ozone standard would expand areas flagged for violating air limits across major producing and refining regions, triggering stricter permits and emissions controls. The bill, sponsored by a Texas Gulf Coast representative, would have delayed or prevented that. Its failure means the industry faces the tightened 2015 ozone standard instead.

industries.industry: Coal-fired power plants and electric utilities
industries.note: Power plants are major emitters of the pollutants that form ozone, and a stricter standard would have expanded nonattainment designations that require costly controls. The bill would have locked in the older, weaker limit until most nonattainment counties cleaned up.

Factories in counties designated as violating ozone limits face new permit conditions and emissions controls. The bill's limits on designating nonattainment areas — direct monitors only, no modeling — would have spared many of them that burden.
